title: Expert serialization congestion — causal trace and mitigation hypotheses
content:
Summary:
This doc captures an investigation into a recurring tail-latency pattern observed on MoE models when running long-context workloads. The root observation is periodic single-expert serialization events that produce 99.9th+ ms spikes even when overall throughput is steady. The goal here is to present a causal trace (what we saw), short experiments that confirm the mechanism, and a set of mitigations we can prototype. This focuses on expert-level IO/serialization rather than scheduler fairness or gating heuristics per se.

Context and motivation:
- Environment: Dedicated pool (r7x-large equivalent), mixed Mistral/Qwen MoE setup via dynamic routing. Models: custom MoE-72B (64 experts in routing layer), long-context evals (8k–32k token windows).
- Workload: synthetic conversation traces and a replay of prod-ish prompt mixes (heavy skew: 85% short, 15% long).
- Symptom window: tail spikes occur roughly every 20–120s, lasting 30–150ms, coinciding with a subset of requests that route to a single hot expert and involve long KV footprints.

What we observed (high level):
1) Packetized timeline: GPU timelines show most kernels within expected bounds, but occasionally a long gap (stall) appears on the networking/PCIe copy timeline that lines up with an expert compute stall.
2) Host trace: threads managing expert IO (expert-io-worker) show serialization; they hold a per-expert mutex for short bursts, but the bursts align with a cache miss on a per-expert activation buffer that triggers a deepcopy + pagefault-like path in our allocator shim.
3) Router/gating stats: gating scores show high concentration for one expert for a small fraction of requests; when that happens the expert's inbound queue length jumps and the worker tries to coalesce but triggers a flush mid-batch.

Reproduction steps (reliable-ish locally):
- Checkout PR branch used for the test: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/2417
- Run the local MoE harness with config: --model moexx72b --route-policy deterministic --long-context 16384 --batch-config max_batch_tokens=4096 --expert-buffer-size=16
- Replay the trace in experiments/long-window-replays/long-heavy.json (attached to PR).
- Collect traces: nvprof/nvtx + eBPF schedtrace + worker logs (enable EXPERT_IO_DEBUG=1)

Representative profiling snippets (abridged):
- nvprof timeline: compute blocks {attn, ffn} ~ 5–12ms each. A PCIe memcpy occasionally takes 68–140ms.
- worker log excerpt (timestamps relative to request start):
  [0.013s] accepted tokens -> route -> expert 17
  [0.015s] enqueue to expert-io-worker-17 (len=1)
  [0.018s] expert worker lock acquired
  [0.018s] observed buffer copy cost ~0.11s (copy + memzero)
  [0.129s] worker flush -> schedule compute on GPU
  [0.190s] compute done, return
  (end tail spike at ~0.19s)
- pprof of host process during spike: top symbols point to allocator::alloc_uninitialized(size) and our utils::aligned_copy_memset

Hypothesis (causal chain):
1) Single-expert hotness (natural in skewed routing + deterministics) leads to repeated small enqueue events for the same expert.
2) Our worker tries to coalesce those enqueues into GPU batches. Coalescing policy currently: flush when either size>threshold OR time>coalesce_ms.
3) When the coalescing window closes, we allocate a fresh contiguous activation buffer on host pinned memory. For large long-context activations this triggers our allocator fallback path that does an extra page-touch/memset to guarantee pinned memory residency (historical correctness for older drivers).
4) That page-touch ends up serialized on the same host core due to the way the worker holds the expert mutex while preparing the buffer, so the allocation and memset block other incoming enqueues for the duration (30–150ms). The net effect is serialized IB/host work causing the observed tail.

Evidence supporting hypothesis:
- Removing the page-touch (temporary patch) significantly reduced the length of the spikes in local repros (median drop from 98ms -> 12ms on the same pattern).
- Changing coalescing policy to allow early flush if mem-alloc predicted size>large_threshold reduced frequency of spikes but increased average token latency slightly (tradeoff).
- Per-expert lock hold time correlates strongly (Spearman rho > 0.8) with observed tail spikes.

Quick experiments and results (numbers are from 3x runs, 95% CI):
- Baseline: 99p latency = 210ms, 99.9p = 480ms (frequent spikes)
- Patch A (disable page-touch): 99p = 200ms, 99.9p = 130ms (-> large improvement)
- Patch B (adaptive coalesce: size-aware early flush): 99p = 215ms, 99.9p = 170ms
- Patch C (per-expert lock -> MPSC queue with lockless handoff): 99p = 205ms, 99.9p = 120ms
Notes: Patch C has more engineering complexity but combines well with Patch B.

Mitigation options (prioritized):
1) Short-term (low-risk): Disable the legacy page-touch path for hosts with modern drivers. Roll as feature flag (EP_DISABLE_PAGE_TOUCH). Requires driver matrix check and can be gated to dedicated pools.
2) Middle-term (moderate): Make coalescing size-aware: if predicted pinned allocation size > X, flush earlier to avoid big host work inside expert mutex. This is adoptable with a config flag and A/B rollout.
3) Long-term (higher effort): Rework expert-io worker to avoid holding per-expert mutex during buffer allocation and page-touch. Move allocation into a prefetch/asynchronous allocator and use lockless MPSC queue for commit. Also consider pre-allocating pinned buffers per-expert based on historical hotness.
4) Platform-level: Router smoothing / jitter injection so hotness for any single expert is less bursty. This would require evaluation for quality/regression risk.

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Skipping page-touch may regress obscure driver edge-cases (older GPUs) where pinned memory was not resident and caused GPU faults; must be feature-flagged and gated.
- Early-flush increases average latency due to smaller batches -> higher per-token GPU overhead -> increased cost. Need to quantify token-cost impact in Optimize.
- Lockless redesign is complex and needs careful correctness proofs for ordering and backpressure.

Next steps (actionable):
- Prod quick-check: enable EP_DISABLE_PAGE_TOUCH in a small dedicated pool (non-critical customers) for 2 weeks and monitor 99.9p and PCIe memcpy prevalence. (Owner: Marina)
- Implement adaptive coalescing prototype in branch: feature/adaptive-coalesce and run cluster perf test (Owner: Jonah).
- Spike: design asynchronous pinned-allocator and microbenchmark (Owner: Priya).
- Add extra observability: per-expert lock-hold histograms, host memcpy NVTX marks, and allocator path telemetry (Owner: Ethan).

Appendix: commands and traces used
- Start harness: ./bin/serve --config conf/moe_long_repro.yaml --route deterministic --trace-id repro-20251104
- Capture nvprof (local repro): NVTX flush + nvprof --profile-from-start off --metrics achieved_occupancy --output-profile repro.nvvp
- Host flame graph (alloc path): sudo perf record -F 99 -g -p $(pidof serving) -- sleep 30; sudo perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.fold; flamegraph.pl out.fold > flame.svg
- Useful logs/flags: EXPERT_IO_DEBUG=1, ALLOC_TRACE=1, EP_DISABLE_PAGE_TOUCH=0/1, COALESCE_MS=8, COALESCE_TOKEN_THRESHOLD=4096

Notes-to-self / open questions:
- How many customers hit this in prod? SRE metrics show ~4 distinct customers with elevated 99.9p correlated to MoE models; need to map to model versions and driver versions.
- Does this interact with cross-device tensor sharding? Early signs: sharded-expert placements can amplify host alloc costs if shards are small.
- Consider a small pre-warm buffer pool sized by exponential moving average of per-expert batch size. 

Document provenance: this is a working investigation; logs and raw traces live in GDrive folder: shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/traces/expert-serialization-repro/ and the PR implementing the page-touch toggle is https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/2417
